client: I just got my chemistry exam back yesterday, and I completely bombed it. I've been pulling all-nighters trying to keep my 4.0, but now that's gone and I feel like such a failure. I don't even know if talking about this will help - it's not like words can change my grade.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really disappointed and defeated after working so hard for that grade. The all-nighters show how much effort you put in, and it's understandable to feel this way when things don't go as planned. What thoughts come up when you tell yourself "I'm a failure" over this one exam?

client: I keep thinking that if I can't maintain perfect grades, I'll never get into a good grad school or have a successful career. It's not just about this one exam - it feels like the first domino falling that will ruin everything I've worked for. I know that sounds dramatic, but that's how my brain keeps spinning it.
therapist: It sounds like this exam has triggered a lot of catastrophic thinking about your future - that one setback means everything will unravel. That must feel really overwhelming to carry. What evidence do you have that contradicts this "domino effect" belief? For example, have you or others you know recovered from setbacks before?

client: Well... my friend Sara failed an entire semester sophomore year and still got into law school. But that's different - she had family connections. I don't have that safety net. It's not just about the grades themselves, it's about how hard I've been pushing myself trying to prove I belong here in the first place.
therapist: It sounds like there's an even deeper layer here - this isn't just about grades, but about proving your worth through perfection. That must add so much pressure to every assignment. When you think about "belonging here," what would it look like if you didn't have to prove it constantly?

client: That's... actually really hard to imagine. If I wasn't constantly trying to prove myself, I guess I'd feel more relaxed and less anxious all the time. But honestly, it feels scary to think about letting go of that mindset - like I'd stop being productive or ambitious altogether. I don't know how to find a middle ground.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two fears - the exhaustion of perfectionism and the worry that letting go might mean losing your drive altogether. That ambivalence makes complete sense. What small experiment could we design to test whether being kinder to yourself actually decreases your ambition, or just makes the journey more sustainable?

client: Maybe I could try giving myself permission to go to bed by midnight for a week instead of pulling all-nighters? But I'm afraid I'll fall behind and do even worse on the next exam. It's frustrating because part of me knows sleep would help, but another part is convinced that's just making excuses to be lazy.
therapist: It sounds like you're wrestling between two very understandable concerns - the real need for rest and the fear that self-care equals laziness. That frustration you're feeling shows how torn you are between these competing beliefs. What if we framed this experiment as collecting data, not just "being kinder" - where you could observe whether adequate sleep actually helps or hurts your performance?

client: I like the idea of treating it like an experiment, but what if the data shows I do worse? That would just confirm all my fears that I need to push myself to the limit. I'm not sure I could handle that proof that I'm not good enough without the extreme effort.
therapist: It sounds like even approaching this as an experiment feels risky because it could confirm your fears about needing to push yourself to extremes. That uncertainty must feel unsettling. What if we broaden what we're measuring in this experiment - not just grades, but also your energy levels, focus, and overall well-being? How might that give a fuller picture of what "good enough" could look like?

client: That actually makes me feel a little defensive, if I'm being honest. Measuring well-being seems nice in theory, but at the end of the day, grad schools and employers only care about the numbers. I don't know how to balance being a real human with also being competitive in this system. It feels like I have to choose.
therapist: I hear how frustrating this feels—like you're being asked to care about things that the system doesn't value, while the stakes (grades, jobs) feel non-negotiable. That tension between being human and being competitive is very real. What would it look like to acknowledge that unfair pressure *while also* finding small ways to prioritize yourself within it—not as a replacement for success, but as part of it?

client: I guess the smallest thing I could try is taking one proper break during study sessions instead of powering through. But honestly, when I imagine doing that, I just hear this voice saying "You're wasting time you could be studying." It's like I can't win either way - either I burn out or I feel guilty for resting.
therapist: It sounds like that critical voice makes even small acts of self-care feel like betrayals—that must be exhausting to carry. The guilt you feel about resting shows how deeply this "all or nothing" mindset has taken root. What if we explored where that voice comes from—when did you first get the message that breaks equal wasted time?

client: I think it started in high school when I saw other kids getting tutors and doing test prep while I was just relying on my own work. I had to push twice as hard to keep up, and now I can't shake the fear that if I relax even a little, I'll fall behind again. But rationally, I know college is different... it's just hard to believe that in my gut.
therapist: It makes so much sense that this fear stuck with you—high school taught you that survival meant constant pushing, and that lesson carried over even though the context changed. That gap between knowing college is different intellectually but not feeling it emotionally must be really frustrating. What would it look like to gently challenge that old narrative this week—maybe by noticing when current evidence contradicts those high school experiences?

client: I could try noticing when classmates take breaks and still do well... but part of me thinks they're just naturally smarter or have some advantage I don't. It's hard to imagine that working for me too. What if my high school mentality was right all along and I really do need to push constantly just to stay afloat?
therapist: It sounds like that old fear is really holding on—this worry that others can afford breaks because they have some innate advantage, while you don't. That must feel incredibly isolating. What if we tested this belief by having you track not just others' breaks, but also their visible effort? You might notice more parallels than you expect.
